extracted.intended_audience: music fans, songwriters, and music/entertainment industry professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Interview-based guidance and evaluative observations about writing pop songs, arranging them for live performance, building tours, and sustaining an artist career. Contains practitioner tips, examples, and reflections rather than formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a great pop record (hookiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s all about hookiness and trying to get as many catchy bits into a song as you possibly can.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great pop records have strong hooks—musical or melodic bits that repeat and stick. Example: packing many choruses into a song because the chorus is often the best part. Aim for multiple memorable moments per track to maximize catchiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bridges to create contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re seeing bridges come back, too... you feel like you’re getting one song and then you get a completely different song.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a bridge or musical flip that changes momentum, introduces a breakdown, or takes the listener somewhere unexpected. Cited influence: Olivia Rodrigo and Dan Nigro’s approach of dramatically flipping sections to keep songs dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include doubt/conflict for emotional interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “All of my favorite songs have a bit of doubt to them... If it was all rosy, it wouldn’t be a great listen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even romantic or upbeat songs benefit from an element of uncertainty or tension. Balance hopeful or happy endings with a thread of doubt or conflict to make songs more emotionally engaging—examples include adding a twist in the lyrics or a darker final line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from lived experience when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you’re going through [love or heartbreak], you can write about them a lot easier. Sometimes I do write observational-type music... but when it comes to love or heartbreak, I find if you’re going through them, you can write about them a lot easier.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal experience yields more authentic and easier-to-write material; observational songwriting is possible but often harder. Use genuine feelings and events as primary material for stronger songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flip the song on its head (songcraft trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I liked flipping the song on its head and making it something different.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deliberate structural or lyrical twist can recontextualize a song and increase impact. Example: ending a catchy chorus with a contradictory final line (e.g., Julia Michaels’ change from 'what a time' to 'what a lie'). Use surprises to subvert expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress pop songs with rock influences for live energy
rubrics_metrics.description: “I write pop songs, but dressing them up in a different way sometimes is quite cool... the rockier stuff really goes off at the shows.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate elements (drum sounds, guitar tones, punchy arrangements) from rock or punk to give pop songs greater live immediacy. Example: chasing a late‑’90s/early‑2000s punk drum sound (Blink-182 influence) to make tracks pop onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about how songs translate live
rubrics_metrics.description: “You’re creating these songs in the head space of how they’re going to translate live.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and arrange with performance in mind—dynamics, sing-along moments, and sections that will land in an arena. Touring experience (seeing reactions in the room) should inform songwriting choices and arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give people value for their money in shows
rubrics_metrics.description: “Giving people value for their money is what I’m trying to do the most.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize setlist selection, production value, and a sense of community to ensure fans feel the concert was worth the price. Ground decisions in fan expectations and communal fandom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance touring with rest to sustain creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: “There’s only so much of yourself that you can give... you need to have a bit of both.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect time away from the road to preserve physical/mental health and allow space for writing. Strategic breaks enable long-term creativity and prevent burnout; examples cited include artists stepping away and returning with strong new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple choruses and repeated hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: “That’s why I’ve got so many choruses in ‘Dinner Party,’ because I felt like it was the best part of the song.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structuring songs with several chorus returns or repeated hooky moments increases memorability. Deliberately lean into repetition where it enhances catchiness rather than dilutes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage trusted songwriting/producers partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: “Songwriters John Ryan and Julian Bunetta worked so much on that album, and you guys continued to have a really strong partnership where they’ve been able to watch you grow over the years.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained collaborations allow co-writers and producers to understand an artist’s evolution and respond sensitively—use long-term partnerships for depth and to revisit/reshape songs (e.g., rewriting 'End of an Era' after events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write songs that evolve inside themselves (dynamic structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It starts off as one type of song and then it turns into a different type of song.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft songs with internal development—changes in mood, tempo, or arrangement within the track keep listeners engaged. Use bridges, breakdowns, or switches in production to create an internal journey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine fan interactions and social media for ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: “There were these postcards at the show with an old tweet... It's like this person is just so powerful in the small things that they do... It was the starting point for ‘Flowers,’ too.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to fans’ stories, tweets, and memorabilia as creative prompts. Small, quirky audience moments can seed lyrical or melodic ideas that resonate widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend genres and regional influences for storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think Irish folk music and country music, they’re married... It’s in us a little bit more... I have always just appreciated the storytelling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elements from related genres (e.g., Irish folk, country) to emphasize narrative and emotional clarity. Genre blending can enrich lyricism and broaden sonic palettes for both recordings and live sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisit and rewrite songs when context changes
rubrics_metrics.description: “We wrote ‘End of an Era’ about four times... it was like, ‘No, we need to return to this,’ after Liam passed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to return to earlier material and reshape it in light of new events or perspectives. Sensitive subjects may require revisiting to better reflect meaning or to serve audiences appropriately.
